::: {#thm-dfs-tree}
#### Depth-first search builds a spanning tree

Let $G$ and $s$ be as in @def-dfs-tree.
Then the depth-first search tree of $G$ from $s$ is a spanning tree (@def-spanning-tree) of $G$.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

Let $S$ be the depth-first search tree, let $n$ be the number of vertices of $G$,
and for each vertex $u \ne s$ let $v(u)$ be the vertex whose call makes the call `dfs(G, u)`.
The call on $v(u)$ starts before the call on $u$, so $v(u) \ne u$.

**$S$ has $n - 1$ edges.**
There is one edge $\set{v(u), u}$ for each of the $n - 1$ vertices $u \ne s$.
If two vertices $u \ne w$ gave the same edge, then $w = v(u)$ and $u = v(w)$,
so the call on $w$ started before the call on $u$, and the call on $u$ started before the call on $w$, which is impossible.

**$S$ is connected.**
By strong induction (@def-strong-induction) on the order in which the calls start,
there is a walk in $S$ from $s$ to each vertex $u$:
for $u = s$ the walk $s$, and for $u \ne s$ a walk from $s$ to $v(u)$, whose call started earlier,
followed by the edge $\set{v(u), u}$.
Two of these walks, one read backward, join any two vertices.

$S$ is connected with $n$ vertices and $n - 1$ edges, so it is a tree by @cor-connected-edges,
and it has every vertex of $G$.

:::

:::
